source_document.subject: mathematics

nodes.label: Solve linear equations
nodes.description: Solve a linear equation by expanding brackets, collecting like terms, rearranging so the variable terms are on one side, dividing, and checking the answer by substituting it back into the original equation.

nodes.label: Equations with variable denominators
nodes.description: Solve a linear equation with the variable in a denominator by multiplying both sides by that denominator, stating the restriction on the variable, and checking the answer by substitution.

nodes.label: Equations with numeric fractions
nodes.description: Solve a linear equation containing fractions with numeric denominators by multiplying the equation by the common denominator, then rearranging, dividing, and checking the answer by substitution.

nodes.label: Write in standard form
nodes.description: Rewrite a quadratic equation given as a product or with terms on both sides in standard form $ax^2+bx+c=0$.

nodes.label: Solve quadratics by factorising
nodes.description: Solve quadratic equations by factorising, giving both solutions, or the single solution when the quadratic is a perfect square (including after dividing out a common factor or rearranging to zero).

nodes.label: Solve equations reducing to quadratics
nodes.description: Solve equations that reduce to a quadratic equation (with fractions and stated restrictions on the variable, bracketed expressions or a fourth power) by rewriting them in the required form and factorising.

nodes.label: Solve by substitution
nodes.description: Solve a system of two linear simultaneous equations by substitution: express one variable in terms of the other, substitute into the second equation, solve, and substitute back to find the other variable.

nodes.label: Solve by elimination
nodes.description: Solve a system of two linear simultaneous equations by elimination: make the coefficients of one variable the same in both equations, add or subtract the equations to eliminate that variable, solve, and substitute back.

nodes.label: Solve graphically
nodes.description: Solve a system of two linear simultaneous equations graphically by drawing both graphs on the same set of axes and reading the coordinates of the point of intersection, and check the answer algebraically.

nodes.label: Word problems: linear equations
nodes.description: Translate a word problem with one unknown quantity into a linear equation, solve it, and state the answer in words.

nodes.label: Word problems: simultaneous equations
nodes.description: Translate a word problem into a system of two linear equations in two unknowns, solve it by substitution, and state the answer in the context of the problem.

nodes.label: Word problems: quadratic equations
nodes.description: Set up a quadratic equation from a word problem, solve it by factorising, and select the solution that satisfies the conditions given in the problem.

nodes.label: Make a variable the subject
nodes.description: Make a variable the subject of a formula by asking what it is joined to and how, and performing the opposite operation on both sides (including after substituting given values).

nodes.label: Take out a common factor
nodes.description: Make a variable the subject of a formula in which it appears in two or more terms by taking it out as a common factor (factorising) and then dividing.

nodes.label: Powers and roots in formulas
nodes.description: Make a variable the subject of a formula when it is squared, cubed or under a square root, by taking the root (with a positive and a negative answer) or squaring both sides.

nodes.label: Clear denominators with the LCD
nodes.description: Solve for a variable that is in a denominator, or in a formula with fractions, by multiplying both sides by the lowest common denominator (LCD) and then continuing to solve.

nodes.label: Solve linear inequalities
nodes.description: Solve a linear inequality in one variable, reversing the inequality sign whenever both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number.

nodes.label: Number line and interval notation
nodes.description: Write down the inequality shown on a number line, and represent the solution of an inequality on a number line and in interval notation, using the correct brackets and the stated number set.

nodes.label: Solve compound inequalities
nodes.description: Solve a compound linear inequality, such as a double inequality or two inequalities joined by "or", and represent the answer on a number line and in interval notation.

questions.stem: Solve for $x$ : $4(2x-9)-4x=4-6x$
solution: Check the answer by substituting the solution back into the original equation: $\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=4[2(4)-9]-4(4)\\&=4(8-9)-16\\&=4(-1)-16\\&=-4-16\\&=-20\\\text{RHS}&=4-6(4)\\&=4-24\\&=-20\\\therefore\text{LHS}=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$ Since both sides are equal, the answer is correct.

questions.stem: Solve for $x$ : $\frac{2-x}{3x+1}=2$
solution: Multiply both sides of the equation by: Division by $\text{0}$ is undefined so there must be a restriction: $\left(x\ne-\frac{1}{3}\right)$ . $\begin{aligned}\frac{2-x}{3x+1}&=2\\(2-x)&=2(3x+1)\end{aligned}$

Check the answer by substituting the solution back into the original equation: $\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\frac{2-(0)}{3(0)+1}\\&=2\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$ Since both sides are equal, the answer is correct.

solution: Divide the equation by common factor: $\begin{aligned}-2{x}^{2}+4x-2&=0\\{x}^{2}-2x+1&=0\end{aligned}$

The quadratic is a perfect square: This is an example of a special situation in which there is only one solution to the quadratic equation because both factors are the same. $\begin{aligned}x-1&=0\\\therefore x&=1\end{aligned}$
Write final answer: The solution to $0=-2{x}^{2}+4x-2$ is $x=1$ .

Solve for $x$ and $y$ : $\begin{aligned}x-y&=1\qquad\ldots(1)\\3&=y-2x\qquad\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$
solution: Use equation to express in terms of: $x=y+1$
Substitute into equation and solve for: $\begin{aligned}3&=y-2\left(y+1\right)\\3&=y-2y-2\\5&=-y\\\therefore y&=-5\end{aligned}$
Substitute back into equation and solve for: $\begin{aligned}x&=(-5)+1\\\therefore x&=-4\end{aligned}$

questions.stem: Solve the following system of equations: $\begin{aligned}4y+3x&=100\qquad\ldots(1)\\4y-19x&=12\qquad\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$
solution: Use either equation to express in terms of: $\begin{aligned}4y+3x&=100\\3x&=100-4y\\x&=\frac{100-4y}{3}\end{aligned}$

Substitute into equation and solve for: $\begin{aligned}4y-19\left(\frac{100-4y}{3}\right)&=12\\12y-19\left(100-4y\right)&=36\\12y-\text{1900}+76y&=36\\88y&=\text{1936}\\\therefore y&=22\end{aligned}$
Substitute back into equation and solve for: $\begin{aligned}x&=\frac{100-4\left(22\right)}{3}\\&=\frac{100-88}{3}\\&=\frac{12}{3}\\\therefore x&=4\end{aligned}$

questions.stem: Solve the following system of equations: $\begin{aligned}3x+y&=2\qquad\ldots(1)\\6x-y&=25\qquad\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$
solution: Make the coefficients of one of the variables the same in both equations: The coefficients of $y$ in the given equations are $\text{1}$ and $-\text{1}$ . Eliminate the variable $y$ by adding equation $\left(1\right)$ and equation $\left(2\right)$ together: $\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{cccc}&3x+y&=&2\\+&6x-y&=&25\\\hline&9x+0&=&27\end{array}\end{aligned}$
Substitute back into either original equation and solve for: $\begin{aligned}3\left(3\right)+y&=2\\y&=2-9\\\therefore y&=-7\end{aligned}$

questions.stem: Solve the following system of equations: $\begin{aligned}2a-3b&=5\qquad\ldots(1)\\3a-2b&=20\qquad\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$
solution: Make the coefficients of one of the variables the same in both equations: By multiplying equation $\left(1\right)$ by $\text{3}$ and equation $\left(2\right)$ by $\text{2}$ , both coefficients of $a$ will be $\text{6}$ . $\begin{aligned}\begin{array}{cccc}&6a-9b&=&15\\-&(6a-4b&=&40)\\\hline&0-5b&=&-25\end{array}\end{aligned}$ (When subtracting two equations, be careful of the signs.)
Substitute value of back into either original equation and solve for: $\begin{aligned}2a-3\left(5\right)&=5\\2a-15&=5\\2a&=20\\\therefore a&=10\end{aligned}$

claims.claim: A linear equation is an equation where the highest exponent of the variable is 1.
Solving an equation means finding the value of the variable that makes the equation true.
To solve an equation, we determine the value of the variable that makes the left hand side equal to the right hand side; for x + 1 = 1 the solution is x = 0.
The solution, also called the root of an equation, is the value of the variable that satisfies the equation.
For linear equations, there is at most one solution for the equation.
To solve equations we use algebraic methods that include expanding expressions, grouping terms, and factorising.
In the general method for solving a linear equation, the first step is to expand all brackets.
Rearrange the terms so that all terms containing the variable are on one side of the equation and all constant terms are on the other side.
Group like terms together and simplify.
Factorise if necessary.
Find the solution and write down the answer.
Check the answer by substituting the solution back into the original equation.
An equation must always be balanced: whatever you do to the left-hand side, you must also do to the right-hand side.
In solving 2x + 2 = 1, the constant is moved to the right-hand side by rearranging, giving 2x = 1 - 2.
After rearranging, simplify: 2x = 1 - 2 becomes 2x = -1.
Divide both sides by 2 to get x = -1/2 from 2x = -1.
To check x = -1/2 in 2x + 2 = 1, substitute it into the left-hand side (2(-1/2) + 2 = -1 + 2 = 1) and compare with the right-hand side, which is 1.
For 4(2x - 9) - 4x = 4 - 6x, expand the brackets and simplify, so that 4(2x - 9) becomes 8x - 36.
In worked example 1, the terms containing x are collected on the left and the constants on the right: 8x - 4x + 6x = 4 + 36, which gives 10x = 40.
Divide both sides by 10 to get x = 4 from 10x = 40.
Substituting x = 4 into the original equation gives -20 on both the left-hand side and the right-hand side; since both sides are equal, the answer is correct.
The book lists an equation with the variable in a denominator, (2 - x)/(3x + 1) = 2, among its examples of linear equations.
To solve (2 - x)/(3x + 1) = 2, multiply both sides of the equation by the denominator, giving (2 - x) = 2(3x + 1).
Division by 0 is undefined, so when the variable is in a denominator there must be a restriction on the variable.
For (2 - x)/(3x + 1) = 2, the stated restriction is x is not equal to -1/3.
Expand the brackets and simplify: 2 - x = 6x + 2 becomes -x - 6x = 2 - 2, which gives -7x = 0.
Divide both sides by -7 to get x = 0/(-7), so x = 0.
Check x = 0 by substituting into the original equation: the left-hand side is (2 - 0)/(3(0) + 1) = 2, which equals the right-hand side; since both sides are equal, the answer is correct.
The book lists an equation containing fractions with numeric denominators, (2a - 3)/3 - 3a = a/3, among its examples of linear equations.
To solve (2a - 3)/3 - 3a = a/3, multiply the equation by the common denominator and simplify, giving 2a - 3 - 9a = a and then -7a - 3 = a.
Rearrange the terms and simplify: -7a - 3 = a becomes -7a - a = 3, which gives -8a = 3.
Divide both sides by -8 to get a = -3/8 from -8a = 3.
Check a = -3/8 by substituting into the original equation: both the left-hand side and the right-hand side equal -1/8; since both sides are equal, the answer is correct.
A quadratic equation is an equation where the exponent of the variable is at most 2.
The equation 2x^2+2x=1 is given as an example of a quadratic equation.
The first step in solving a quadratic equation is to rewrite the equation in the required form ax^2+bx+c=0.
Quadratic equations differ from linear equations in that a linear equation has only one solution, while a quadratic equation has at most two solutions.
There are some special situations in which a quadratic equation has either one solution or no solutions.
Quadratic equations are solved using factorisation.
To solve a quadratic equation by factorisation, write it in its equivalent factorised form; for example, 2x^2-x-3=0 is written as (x+1)(2x-3)=0.
If a times b equals 0, then a=0 or b=0.
Divide the entire equation by any common factor of the coefficients to obtain an equation of the form ax^2+bx+c=0.
After dividing out the common factor, a, b and c have no common factors.
For example, 2x^2+4x+2=0 can be written as x^2+2x+1=0 after dividing by the common factor.
Factorise ax^2+bx+c=0 to be of the form (rx+s)(ux+v)=0.
The two solutions come from setting each factor equal to zero: (rx+s)=0 or (ux+v)=0.
The solutions of (rx+s)(ux+v)=0 are x=-s/r or x=-v/u, respectively.
Check the answer by substituting it back into the original equation.
To solve 3x^2+2x-1=0, factorise it as (x+1)(3x-1)=0.
After factorising, solve for both factors: x+1=0 gives x=-1, OR 3x-1=0 gives x=1/3.
Write the final answer as a statement giving both solutions: the solution to 3x^2+2x-1=0 is x=-1 or x=1/3.
An equation written as 0=-2x^2+4x-2 is rearranged to -2x^2+4x-2=0, with zero on the right, before dividing out the common factor to give x^2-2x+1=0.
Divide the equation by the common factor: -2x^2+4x-2=0 becomes x^2-2x+1=0.
Factorise x^2-2x+1=0 as (x-1)(x-1)=0, which is written (x-1)^2=0.
When both factors are the same, as in (x-1)(x-1)=0, the quadratic is a perfect square.
When the quadratic is a perfect square, there is only one solution to the quadratic equation because both factors are the same.
For a perfect square, solve the single repeated factor: (x-1)^2=0 gives x-1=0, so x=1; the solution to 0=-2x^2+4x-2 is x=1.
When solving for two unknown variables, two equations are required, and these equations are known as simultaneous equations.
The solutions of simultaneous equations are the values of the unknown variables which satisfy both equations simultaneously.
If there are n unknown variables, then n independent equations are required to obtain a value for each of the n variables.
Substitution, step 1: use the simplest of the two given equations to express one of the variables in terms of the other.
Substitution, step 2: substitute the expression into the second equation.
Substituting into the second equation reduces the number of equations and the number of variables by one, leaving one equation with one unknown variable which can be solved.
Substitution, final step: use the solution to substitute back into the first equation to find the value of the other unknown variable.
Worked example 6: equation (1), x - y = 1, is used to express x in terms of y, giving x = y + 1.
Worked example 6: substituting x = y + 1 into equation (2), 3 = y - 2x, gives 3 = y - 2(y + 1), which is solved to give y = -5.
Worked example 6: substituting y = -5 back into x = y + 1 gives x = (-5) + 1, so x = -4.
Worked example 6: the final answer is x = -4 and y = -5.
Worked example 7: either equation may be used to express a variable in terms of the other; equation (1), 4y + 3x = 100, is rearranged to 3x = 100 - 4y and then to x = (100 - 4y)/3.

Worked example 7: when the substituted expression is a fraction, multiply both sides by its denominator to clear it, so 4y - 19((100 - 4y)/3) = 12 becomes 12y - 19(100 - 4y) = 36, which is solved to give y = 22.
Worked example 7: substituting y = 22 back into x = (100 - 4y)/3 gives x = (100 - 88)/3 = 12/3, so x = 4.
Worked example 7: the final answer is x = 4 and y = 22.
Elimination, step 1: make the coefficients of one of the variables the same in both equations.
Worked example 8: the coefficients of y in the two equations are 1 and -1, so adding equation (1) and equation (2) together eliminates the variable y.
Worked example 8: after eliminating y, the resulting equation 9x = 27 is solved to give x = 3.
Worked example 8: substitute the value of x back into either original equation and solve for the other variable; 3(3) + y = 2 gives y = -7.
Worked example 8: the final answer is x = 3 and y = -7.
Worked example 9: when the coefficients are not already equal, multiply the equations by suitable numbers; multiplying equation (1) by 3 and equation (2) by 2 makes both coefficients of a equal to 6.
Worked example 9: with equal coefficients of a (6a - 9b = 15 and 6a - 4b = 40), subtracting the second equation from the first eliminates a and leaves 0 - 5b = -25.
When subtracting two equations, be careful of the signs.
Worked example 9: after eliminating a, -5b = -25 is solved by dividing -25 by -5, giving b = 5.
Worked example 9: substitute the value of b back into either original equation and solve for the other variable; 2a - 3(5) = 5 gives 2a = 20, so a = 10, and the final answer is a = 10 and b = 5.
Simultaneous equations can be solved graphically: if the graphs of each linear equation are drawn, the solution to the system is the coordinates of the point at which the two graphs intersect.
Graphical method, step 1: write both equations with y expressed in terms of x (for example 4y + 3x = 100 becomes y = -(3/4)x + 25, and 4y - 19x = 12 becomes y = (19/4)x + 3).
Graphical method, step 2: sketch the graphs of both equations on the same set of axes.
Graphical method, step 3: find the coordinates of the point of intersection of the two graphs; in worked example 10 they intersect at (4, 22).
Graphical method, final step: read the solution from the intersection point; in worked example 10 the final answer is x = 4 and y = 22.
The point of intersection is written with a semicolon between the coordinates; the intersection (2, 1) gives the solution x = 2 and y = 1.
A solution read from a graph can be checked using algebraic methods.
Checking algebraically, step 1: substitute equation (1), x = 2y, into equation (2).
Checking algebraically, step 3: substitute the value of y back into equation (1), giving x = 2(1) = 2.
The graphical method and the algebraic method give the same solution.
Checking algebraically, step 2: solve y - 4y = -3, which gives -3y = -3 and so y = 1.
To solve a word problem, write a set of equations that represent the problem mathematically.
The solution of the equations that represent the problem is the solution to the word problem.
Problem solving strategy, step 1: read the whole question and identify what we are asked to solve for.
Problem solving strategy, step 2: assign a variable, for example x, to the unknown quantity.
Problem solving strategy, step 3: translate the words into algebraic expressions by rewriting the given information in terms of the variable.
Problem solving strategy, step 4: set up an equation or system of equations to solve for the variable.
Problem solving strategy, step 5: solve the equation algebraically using substitution.
Problem solving strategy, step 6: check the solution.

A bicycle has two wheels and a tricycle has three wheels, so 19 wheels in total gives the equation 2b + 3t = 19, labelled (2).

Substitute the value of j back into b = j + 2 and solve for b: b = 6 + 2 = 8.

A literal equation is an equation that has several letters or variables.
The area of a circle is an example of a literal equation: A = πr².
The formula for speed is an example of a literal equation: v = D/t.
Solving literal equations is also known as changing the subject of the formula.
Literal equations are solved in terms of one variable.
Solving literal equations uses the principles learnt about solving equations, applied to rearranging literal equations.
To isolate the unknown variable, ask "what is it joined to?" and "how is it joined?"
After finding what the unknown variable is joined to and how, perform the opposite operation to both sides as a whole.
If the unknown variable is in two or more terms, take it out as a common factor.
When the square root of both sides is taken, remember that there will be a positive and a negative answer.
If the unknown variable is in the denominator, multiply both sides by the lowest common denominator (LCD) and then continue to solve.
LCD is the abbreviation for lowest common denominator.
The area of a triangle is A = ½bh.
To isolate the required variable, rearrange the equation with that variable on one side of the equals sign and the rest of the variables on the other.
To make h the subject of A = ½bh, the book rearranges to 2A = bh and then to 2A/b = h.
The height of a triangle is given by h = 2A/b.
To make R the subject of h = R × H/(R + r²), the first step clears the denominator R + r² by multiplying both sides by it, giving h(R + r²) = R × H.
After clearing the denominator, continue to solve by expanding the bracket: h(R + r²) becomes hR + hr², giving hR + hr² = HR.
When R appears in more than one term, collect the terms containing R on one side: hr² = HR − hR.
Take R out as a common factor of the terms on that side: hr² = R(H − h).
After factorising, dividing by (H − h) gives R = hr²/(H − h).
A linear inequality is similar to a linear equation in that the largest exponent of a variable is 1.
The methods used to solve linear inequalities are similar to those used to solve linear equations.
The only difference between solving an inequality and solving an equation occurs when there is a multiplication or a division that involves a minus sign.
Dividing both sides of 8>6 by -2 gives -4>-3, which is not true, so the inequality sign must be switched around, giving -4<-3.
When we divide or multiply both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the direction of the inequality changes.
For example, if x<1, then -x>-1.
We cannot divide or multiply an inequality by a variable.
To solve the inequality 2x+2<=1, rearrange to 2x<=1-2, simplify to 2x<=-1, and then x<=-1/2.
For an equation such as 2x+2=1 there is only a single value of x for which the equation is true.
For an inequality there is a range of values for which the inequality is true; this is the main difference between an equation and an inequality.
The answer to an equation or an inequality can be represented on a number line.
In interval notation an interval is written with its two endpoints separated by a semicolon inside brackets, for example (4, 12).
Round brackets indicate that the number is not included.
A square bracket indicates that the number is included.
Round brackets are always used for positive and negative infinity.
The interval (4, 12) includes all real numbers greater than but not equal to 4 and less than but not equal to 12.
The interval (-infinity;-1) includes all real numbers less than, but not equal to, -1.
The interval [1, 13) includes all real numbers greater than or equal to 1 and less than but not equal to 13.
Interval notation can only be used to represent an interval of real numbers.
The answer x<=-1/2 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;-1/2].
To solve 6-r>2, rearrange and solve for -r: -r>2-6, giving -r>-4.
From -r>-4, multiply and reverse the inequality sign, giving r<4.
The solution r<4 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;4).
To solve 4q+3<2(q+3), first expand the bracket, giving 4q+3<2q+6.
Rearrange and solve for q: 4q+3<2q+6 becomes 4q-2q<6-3, giving 2q<3.
Divide both sides of 2q<3 by 2, giving q<3/2, with the inequality sign unchanged.
The solution q<3/2 is represented in interval notation as (-infinity;3/2).
To solve the compound inequality 5<=x+3<8, subtract 3 from all the parts of the inequality, giving 2<=x<5.
The answer to a compound inequality such as 2<=x<5 is represented on a number line.
The solution 2<=x<5 is represented in interval notation as [2, 5).
